subject: arts-music
lesson_title: Independent application A: notation or sequencing
task_label: Music theory and listening — Independent application
essential_question: How can understanding music creation and performance help us explain, decide, create, or solve something that matters?
learning_objectives: Apply notation or sequencing independently in a new representation, text, situation, or design constraint.
Use subject-appropriate evidence or representation to communicate understanding of notation or sequencing.
Check, revise, or improve work about notation or sequencing using stated success criteria.
lesson_success_criteria: The learner completes the central task about notation or sequencing.
The learner gives evidence, reasoning, a model, or a documented process rather than an unsupported answer.
The learner checks or revises the work and can identify a next step.
materials: unit-specific source, model, manipulatives, safe materials, or approved digital tool

Household-accessible route: pencil or pen and scrap paper are enough. For sound or performance work, tap, clap, use spoken syllables, move a finger, or notate silently. Specialized art materials, instruments, paid software, cameras, microphones, and recording devices are optional and never affect credit.
task_brief: Day 4 of "Music Creation and Performance" (unit 3, grade 7) is an independent application on notation or sequencing. It is one step inside the unit — not the whole unit project — and takes about 40–60 minutes. The unit is working toward: Compose, arrange, or perform a short piece with a score, sequence, or listening guide. Today's work contributes to that by handling notation or sequencing at the independent application a stage, against the unit's wider topics of rhythm and meter, melody and harmony concepts, form, and notation or sequencing. This session produces reviewable evidence toward the unit performance task.
primary_task: Independently make one short original piece built around notation or sequencing, aiming at an effect you choose in advance. Write the intended effect first, in one sentence, before you begin. Make the piece, then step back and judge honestly whether the effect landed, citing the specific element that carries it and one element that works against it. Revise that second element and keep both versions. The work must be your own; a tutor may demonstrate technique or give feedback but must not make any part of the graded piece. Anchor today's work inside its unit: this session's evidence is about notation or sequencing, and it belongs to "Music Creation and Performance", which also covers separate topics such as rhythm and meter. Close out with this check before you stop: In one concise response, show or explain the most important idea about notation or sequencing; then identify one check that would catch an error or weak claim. At grade 7 the bar is independent work with reasoning that a reader can follow without you present, plus one stated check you ran on your own result before submitting.
requirements: Meet this lesson's own success criteria: The learner completes the central task about notation or sequencing., The learner gives evidence, reasoning, a model, or a documented process rather than an unsupported answer., and The learner checks or revises the work and can identify a next step.
Address the lesson objective: Apply notation or sequencing independently in a new representation, text, situation, or design constraint.
Produce the deliverable for an independent application: One original short piece, a pre-written intent statement, a two-element self-critique, and a revision with both versions kept.
Show the process, not only the result — a working log, draft, or annotated study.
Complete the critique criteria list in this package before submitting.
deliverable: One original short piece, a pre-written intent statement, a two-element self-critique, and a revision with both versions kept.
critique_criteria: The intended effect was written in one sentence before work began.
The finished piece is original and uses the lesson's focus to pursue that effect.
The self-critique cites one element that carries the intent and one that works against it.
A revision of the weaker element exists and both versions are kept.
The graded piece is the student's own authorship; assistance did not make any part of it.

presentation_and_privacy.presentation_options: You choose the audience. Keeping the work entirely to yourself, showing it to one parent or trusted adult, or submitting it as a file with no one watching are all full-credit options. No public performance, exhibition, class presentation, live audience, photograph, camera, or voice recording is required at any point in this task, and choosing the most private option never lowers the score.
presentation_and_privacy.text_or_no_audio_alternative: A written alternative is always available and scores the same. Instead of performing, speaking, or recording, you may submit a written description of what you made or would make, a notated or diagrammed version, a labelled plan, or a written analysis covering the same criteria. Nothing in this task requires a working microphone, camera, or the ability to perform aloud.

copyright_and_authorship: The graded submission must be your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI tool may explain an idea, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but must not produce, write, debug, or make any part of the work that is scored. Any material you did not create yourself must be in the public domain, openly licensed, or used as a short cited excerpt for study — reproduce no more than the point requires, credit the maker and the source, and never copy full lyrics, a complete score, or a whole image and present it as your own.
accessibility_options: Provide readable text plus optional audio or read-aloud support; no voice feature is required.
Chunk directions into one action at a time and show a worked example or model.
Allow typed, handwritten, spoken, drawn, manipulatives-based, or demonstrated responses when the standard permits.
Offer reduced-copying, extended-time, hidden-timer, movement-break, and low-distraction options.
Use captions, alt text, high-contrast print, keyboard access, and text-only fallbacks for media.
Preserve the learning target while adjusting quantity, pacing, representation, or response mode.
task_accessibility_provisions: This task centres a visual element (notation or sequencing). Provide tactile, raised-line, or high-relief equivalents, enlarged and high-contrast print, and a verbal description route. Never make colour discrimination alone carry a criterion — pair any colour judgement with value, label, or texture.

This work spans sessions, so supply a written milestone plan, explicit checkpoint dates, and a task breakdown. Executive-function load — sequencing, holding the plan in mind, remembering where the work stopped — must not become a silent part of what is being assessed.
Breaks, extended time, a hidden timer, reduced copying, and a low-distraction setting are available on request and never reduce the score.
safety_and_privacy_rules: Allow a pause, break, or alternate response mode without treating it as failure.
Protect hearing, ventilation, tool safety, copyright, cultural context, and respectful representation.
Provide a non-performance or low-audience option when needed without lowering the academic target.

media.suggestion: Optional diagram, map, worked example, source image, demonstration, or short clip supporting notation or sequencing.
media.fallback: Provide the same information as readable steps, alt text, transcript, tactile/concrete model, or teacher demonstration.

remediation: Reteaching for notation or sequencing follows the signal actually observed, not a fixed script. If the signal is "prerequisite gap": Return to the smallest prerequisite needed for notation or sequencing, model it with a concrete or text-only representation, then retry one fresh item. If the signal is "procedure without understanding": Ask the learner to explain or represent why the process for notation or sequencing works before continuing. If the signal is "correct but low confidence": Confirm the reasoning specifically, offer one varied example of notation or sequencing, and avoid unnecessary remediation. If the signal is "repeated error pattern": Name the observable pattern neutrally, contrast it with a worked example, and schedule a short same-day or next-session review. If the signal is "mastery evidence": Require accurate independent application plus explanation on a later or different occasion before marking notation or sequencing mastered. Re-check with one fresh item of the same kind before moving on, and record which signal was seen so the pattern is visible across the unit rather than treated as a one-off.
extension: Apply notation or sequencing under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or teach the idea with an original example without completing another learner’s graded work. Treat this as optional depth on notation or sequencing rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same. Extension work stays private by default and uses only original, public-domain, or properly cited material. Extension work is never required to reach mastery and must not be assigned as a penalty.
